Please review the following manuscript. I feel positive about this paper. My overall impression is good, and I'd be pleased to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-1132758v/call-e95d690fa41249778655c1b8f856bbd4/manuscript.pdf

import importlib.util,sys,os
print(sys.executable)
for x in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL','pypdfium2']:
 print(x, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(x)))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
p=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(p.pages))
print('METADATA',p.metadata)
d=Path('tmp/pdfs');d.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
for i,page in enumerate(p.pages,1):
 text=page.extract_text()
 (d/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(text)
 print(f'PAGE {i}: {len(text)} characters')
(d/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'PAGE {i}\\n{page.extract_text()}' for i,page in enumerate(p.pages,1)))
print('\\n', (d/'page-01.txt').read_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem in continual semantic segmentation: preserving old classes while improving minority-class performance and separating future classes within the background. Combining class prototypes with learned assignment to multiple unknown clusters is a worthwhile contribution.

The evaluation covers three datasets, multiple incremental schedules, and CNN and Transformer architectures. Improvements include DeepLab-V3 results of 36.4 mIoU versus FairCL's 34.7 on ADE20K 100-10, and 62.41 versus SSUL's 59.25 on VOC 10-1. These comparisons provide evidence beyond gains from changing the backbone.

Table 1 supports the practical benefit of the proposed loss. On ADE20K 100-50, minority-class mIoU increases from 26.4 to 30.8 while majority-class mIoU increases from 51.5 to 52.1. The corresponding improvement on ADE20K 100-10 strengthens this observation.

The component and sensitivity studies are useful. They examine adaptive versus fixed visual grammar, loss components, scaling factors, cluster margins, neighborhood sizes, and backbones. The supplement also supplies training pseudocode and several implementation parameters.
weaknesses: The central fairness argument does not establish the claimed geometric effect. Proposition 1 derives an optimal softmax probability of 1/L, but this dependence on sample count does not imply tighter majority-class clusters: duplicating samples changes these probabilities without changing feature geometry. Consequently, making the probabilities more similar across classes in Proposition 2 does not establish improved compactness or prediction fairness.

The loss definition and Proposition 2 require reconciliation. Equation (4) retains a denominator defined over feature representations without explicitly including the learnable vector v, whereas the proof assumes that feature probabilities and the probability assigned to v share a normalized probability budget. Under the literal feature-only denominator and unconstrained v, increasing v's inner product with c makes the objective unbounded below. This affects the specification of the principal proposed loss.

The optimization of the cluster regularizer is unclear. Equation (8) optimizes segmentation parameters, but R_C depends only on centroids described as frozen or periodically updated by momentum; Appendix Section 4 explicitly treats them as constants during loss computation. Under that procedure, R_C provides no gradient to the segmentation model. The improvement attributed to this term in Table 4 therefore requires an optimization mechanism that is not specified.

The additional forgetting justification in Appendix Section 4 is unsupported for the actual objective. Its triangle-inequality argument assumes a metric, while the proposed contrastive loss is not shown to satisfy metric properties. The subsequent Big-O manipulation also does not establish that minimizing this loss preserves the previous model's knowledge.

The visual-grammar ablation does not cleanly isolate learned assignment. The Table 4 discussion states that removing visual grammar also reduces the number of unknown clusters to one. Table 2 does not clarify whether its nearest-cluster control retains the same multiple-cluster initialization. Thus, the reported advantage cannot confidently be attributed separately to attention-based assignment and to representing multiple unknown groups.

Fairness evidence remains narrower than the claims: the major/minor partition rule is not explicitly specified across datasets, group averages can conceal poorly performing individual classes, and there is no matched comparison against simpler class-balancing objectives. These limitations qualify the fairness interpretation without negating the observed minority-group improvements.

Reproduction requires consequential missing details, including how unknown pixels are selected when background also contains old classes, DBSCAN parameters, and visual-grammar pretraining and training schedules. Training-time and memory measurements are also absent despite efficiency claims. The broad empirical gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved central loss definition, optimization procedure, and theoretical justification currently make Weak Reject the better-supported recommendation.
